content.summary_of_the_paper: This is evaluate CLIP on the continue learning setting and shows it performs better than the existing method on five benchmarks. In class-incremental setting, domain-incremental setting, and task-agnostic setting, the method shows consistent improvement. The paper shows that large-scale models are good for continual learning tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The paper evaluates CLIP model on a number of continual learning tasks and shows its effectiveness. The method is simple and achieves better performance, which is an important benchmark to be known by the community.
2. The paper is clearly written.

Weakness:
1. Unfair comparison: the paper compares CLIP with a number of continual learning tasks, yet CLIP model has been trained on a much large scale of data. A higher performance is expected given that CLIP has seen so much data.

2. Lack of insight in the experiment: This paper just uses CLIP to evaluate the continual learning task in a zero-shot manner, which is an evaluation method that is known. The author should teach the community new knowledge on how to use CLIP better than just zero-shot.

3. Method is not that interesting. As the author said, this is a simple baseline, which is expected and should be fine for a technique report. The author should consider adding some new things in using CILP smarter and make it more effective than the vanilla CLIP.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written and reproducible. Yet it lacks some novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper shows the effectiveness of using CLIP in continual learning setting, however, due to the unfair comparison and lack of insight, I vote for rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of continual learning under diverse scenarios, with a frozen semantic-rich pre-trained representation model, CLIP. The authors claim that the catastrophic forgetting problem is already well addressed with the CLIP, without any fine-tunung upon incremental phases, and only with zero-shot evaluation. The experimental results on various benchmarks show the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strengths
    - First of all, the proposed framework demonstrates better performance than other baselines for the standard benchmarks.
    - The proposed framework does not require any fine-tuning procedure, which is a critical part of many existing continual learning frameworks.
    - The experimental results in this paper can be served as a baseline for the future.
    - The paper is well-written and clear.
    
- Weaknesses
    - My major concern for this work is that this work is just a combination of naive evaluations of CLIP.
    - First, it is well-known that CLIP presents impressive zero-shot classification performances for image recognition. So the reported results are not surprising, since each incremental test set is just a subset of entire datasets. Obviously, CLIP is trained with 400M scale datasets, which makes CLIP a super-semantic rich model. Moreover, LAION 400M datasets consist of images from diverse domains, domain-incremental performance is also easily expected. Therefore, the reported results are somewhat easily expected, while it is the first work to properly reported them.
    - For me, the title is also not proper, since in this work there is no **continual learner**.
    
    - Minor
        - Typo : WE → We (Last sentence of Section 3 Methodology).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity : The paper is well-written and clear
- Quality : The presentation of the paper is neat.
- Novelty : The main weakness of this submission, as mentioned in the Weakness section.
- Reproducibility : I think the paper provides sufficient information to reproduce the result.
content.summary_of_the_review: Despite its potential to be served as the baseline, I hardly agree that this submission meets the bar of ICLR, as stated in the weakness section.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper evaluates the performance of a pretrained, frozen CLIP model (Radford et al. 2021) in a variety of continual classification learning settings, demonstrating outperformance relative to a number of baseline methods, including SOTA in many settings. Since CLIP works by scoring the similarity between image and text embeddings, a choice has to be made of how to map class labels to text, in terms of the fixed prompt used and the textural description of each task - in the paper, an analysis is run of the effect of different class -> text mappings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- The key strength of this paper is the combination of (i) the simplicity of the method proposed, in the sense that it requires no extra training and essentially uses the pretrained CLIP model out of the box, and (ii) the very strong performance it shows compared to SOTA methods in a wide variety of continual classification tasks.
- The paper is well written with a clearly described set of experiments and a good analysis on the prompting protocol used.

Opportunities for improvement
- While the paper demonstrates that CLIP is an important and powerful baseline for continual learning benchmarks, and for this reason it is a valuable piece of work, the approach nevertheless does not respect the constraints that are typically imposed on continual learning methods and this fact warrants some discussion, of which there is little to none in the paper. For example:
    - As is clearly recapped in the paper, continual learning is concerned with learning from non stationary data, but CLIP is trained on a huge dataset that is i.i.d. before deployed in a continual learning setting, while most continual learning methods are trained from scratch from non stationary data.
    - One could argue that CLIP is not doing any continual learning, it has just been trained on such a large amount of data in the standard way that it can already perform all the tasks in the continual learning benchmarks - hence it does not need to learn them. 
    - This begs the question: does CLIP render continual learning obsolete because it knows everything it will ever need to know? Could such a general representation exist? Arguably, the main premise of continual learning is that it does not, in the sense that the assumption is that the algorithm is constantly faced with new data/experiences that it must learn from and may not necessarily have developed the right abstractions for. There are no easy answers to these questions, I just think that it is important to raise the potential problems with proposing a fixed model as a solution to continual learning.
    - Another question worth addressing is whether there could possibly have been leakage from CLIP’s training set to the datasets used in the CL benchmarks in the paper. In a softer sense, perhaps the CL benchmarks are too in-distribution to CLIP’s training set for them to be considered valid or interesting tests for continual learning.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written, the evaluation of CLIP on CL benchmarks is novel as far as I am aware. No code seems to have been provided in order to reproduce the results, but they should be able to be checked quite readily since they are using a published model.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper provides a valuable, very strong, and simple baseline for continual learning benchmarks in the form of a pretrained CLIP model that is frozen and deployed out of the box. It furthers the question of to what extent frozen pretrained models are enough for continual learning. The key weakness of the paper is a failure to adequately discuss the limitations and consequences of such an approach, one that breaks the standard constraints for CL methods can not actually learn from new data - rather it is based on the assumption that it already knows everything and so does not need to learn. I think the paper would benefit greatly from including a timely discussion to this effect (perhaps addressing some of the points raised in the previous section)- in the advent of large pretrained models and in the context of such a strong set of results to provoke the issue. I’d be willing to increase my score if this was added to the paper.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes to use CLIP trained model as a solution to the continual learning problem. In a zero-shot fashion, prompts are constructed for each seen class and then predictions are made accordingly. 
The paper shows that using CLIP pretrained models outperforms all continual learning baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
-  Evaluating such a strong model on downstream tasks under continual learning setting is interesting. 
-  Showing that CLIP model provides strong results under the continual evaluations protocols.

Weaknesses:

- I am not sure what is exactly novel in this paper: authors of CLIP have already shown impressive zero-shot performance on a large variety of downstream tasks including those that are used in this paper. As such a superior performance is to be expected when you add classes incremental (since model is frozen). 
Continual Learning is about continually updating and improving the learned model including the representation. It is normal that using a model trained on 400M image-text pairs would perform better than continual learning methods trained from scratch on cifar10 for example. 
- What would be more interesting is to show if CLIP representation can be further improved by continual learning e.g., start from this backbone. 
- It is unclear how the compared methods are implemented and whether they started from a randomly initialized model or from a pretrained model.
- The paper lacks discussion on possible failure scenarios or possible directions for continual learning or evaluations. 
- It is unclear what is the effect of using the bad and good prompts for the different datasets.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Originality

 - [1] Had already studied the performance of strong pretrained models under continual learning setting and further proposed a continual learning method. I am not sure how novel is the paper compared to [1].

Clarity:

- Some details are missing e.g., discussion of compared methods and their hyper-parameters. 





[1] Ostapenko O, Lesort T, Rodrıguez P, Arefin MR, Douillard A, Rish I, Charlin L. Continual Learning with Foundation Models: An Empirical Study of Latent Replay. CoLLAs. 2022..
content.summary_of_the_review:
While it is interesting to show that CLIP model can be used for continual learning of different tasks and might be used as off the shelf solution, the paper doesn't go beyond that. There is no discussion on the effect of how close the task distribution is to CLIP. It is unclear whether applying any of the studied continual learning methods on top of CLIP would improve the performance over the frozen model or not. 
To this reviewer, the paper is a starting point but in its current form doesn't provide any strong conclusion or evidence to the community.
